title: Putting the parts together: muskets and mass production

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In modern mass production techniques, the different stages of the manufacturing process must be carefully considered in order to produce objects of the required quality, while keeping costs as low as possible. A ballpoint pen, for example, is so cheap that when it runs out of ink you can throw it away and get a new one. This is possible because machines exist that can make the component parts for millions of pens, and then assemble them together. But a critical fact here is that all the parts of one kind must be exactly the same size and shape so that they are interchangeable. For example, a ballpoint pen has a metal ball that conveys the ink to the paper. It would cause major problems in assembly if some of the metal balls were made even a fraction too big or too small. If they are all manufactured to exactly the right dimensions, however, then any ball will fit in any pen, and assembly can be done easily and rapidly. In engineering this is known as ‘close-tolerance interchangeability’, and it has been achieved only after a long and stony path. It is now the main difference between industrial manufacture, where identical components are produced on a large scale by machine, and production by craftsmen who produce individual components which may each have slight variations.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Tremendous efforts were made to achieve interchangeability in the state armaments industry of eighteenth-century France in order to speed up the manufacture of guns, but with very limited success. The soldier’s weapon of the time was a type of gun called a muzzle-loaded musket. It was loaded by pouring gunpowder into the gun, and pushing the ball (the precursor of the modern bullet) down on top. The gunpowder charge was detonated by a spark caused by a flint striking a steel plate, and this ‘flint lock’ was a critical sub-system of the gun. The flint lock was a complex mechanism consisting of about twenty different parts, and to equip a large army with muskets, many thousands of them had to be produced. This task was the job of the locksmith.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Locksmiths first produced the separate parts from iron, and then complete locks were made by sorting through piles of component parts to find a combination that could be made to fit together and work-although the locksmiths usually had to make further small changes to individual pieces by filing the metal to make them fit one another exactly. Thus every lock was an individual mechanism produced by a craftsman, and the parts were rarely interchangeable between locks. Imagine how unfeasible such methods would be for the manufacture of the ballpoint pen.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Production rates using such methods were very slow, so there were several hundred craftsmen in the trade working in small groups in workshops scattered around the armament factories. Locksmiths were highly skilled, and would protect their own interests, which they naturally saw as preserving the status quo. However, in 1723 in Paris, Guillaume Deschamps came up with a proposal for a new system of production. The inventor, disassembled fifty flint locks and recombined their parts to produce fifty functioning flint locks. The minister of war ordered Valliere [director general of artillery] to supervise Deschamps’ attempts to expand his system. By 1727 Deschamps had manufactured 660 locks judged interchangeable by Valliere’s own inspectors, ‘all properly reassembled with a single stroke of the file’. Each lock, however, had cost five times the current price. Undaunted, Deschamps proposed a much larger manufacture to produce 5000 identical locks, which he expected to cost only one twentieth of the current price. Tasks were to be divided among specialist workers, who would use precision tools to shape parts to exact measurements. Master pattern locks would be distributed to the War Office, inspector, controller and examiner. Deschamps noted that with six hundred locksmiths in the St Etienne region, he could manufacture 40,000 flint locks a year. (Alder, 1999, p221)

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: In fact none of this came to pass. In spite of the advantages of the new process, both in the initial assembly of guns and in their subsequent repair, especially in the field of battle, it was by no means clear that productivity could be increased or costs brought down. Indeed, it took locksmiths longer to make the parts, since they had to match very precise specifications. The locksmiths were also less than co-operative towards the introduction of the new process, fearing that their craft was being de-skilled so that they would lose their powerful position. Nor was it easy to solve the administrative and technical problems of organising the new specialists involved in the manufacturing process, who sometimes lived in widely dispersed areas.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Fifty years later we read of Honore Blanc, controller of musket production at three factories in France, repeating the demonstration of interchangeability with the locks of the standard French musket known as the Mi777. The same arguments raged and little was done. But eventually interchangeability of flint-lock parts was achieved on a large scale at Blanc’s own manufacturing base. New divisions of labour and new machines contrived to keep the costs of interchangeable locks to only 30% greater than the individual locks made by the old methods. When Napoleon’s armies marched across Europe at the beginning of the nineteenth century, the basis of mass production had been established.
